overview: This file documents U.S. policy toward foreign books and other mass media in occupied Japan during the second half of 1946. It begins with the Foreign Policy Association's request to authorize a Japanese translation of Mr. Hart's booklet, Eclipse of the Rising Sun, and the State Department's explanation that publication required occupation-authority licensing despite presenting no policy objection. A second correspondence concerns Admiral Kichisaburō Nomura's attempt, through Compton Pakenham, to send Eleanor Roosevelt his Japanese-language book A Mission to America; Department officials advised Roosevelt not to acknowledge a delivery that circumvented postal restrictions. The largest component is a U.S. Political Adviser despatch transmitting SCAP Circular No. 12 and its four enclosures, which prescribe licensing, payment, copyright, censorship, importation, and distribution rules for foreign magazines, books, films, news and photograph services, performances, and non-commercial media in Japan. A later administrative charge-out sheet concludes the bundle.

subfiles.title: Foreign Policy Association inquiry about Eclipse of the Rising Sun
subfiles.to: John Carter Vincent, Far Eastern Division, Department of State
subfiles.about: Wilgus asks whether a Tokyo firm may translate and publish Mr. Hart's Eclipse of the Rising Sun and whether the State Department has any policy objection.
subfiles.summary: A Tokyo firm wishes to obtain Japanese publication rights to Mr. Hart's booklet. Walter Wilgus asks for confirmation that American books may be published in Japan and requests a Department review of the work before the Foreign Policy Association grants the rights.

subfiles.title: State Department reply on publishing Eclipse of the Rising Sun in Japan
subfiles.from: Henry P. Leverich, Acting Chief, Division of Occupied Areas
subfiles.about: Leverich explains the occupation procedures governing publication of the booklet in Japan and states that the Department has no policy objection.
subfiles.summary: The reply says that Japanese nationals are temporarily prohibited from direct business relations with foreign-owned concerns. Wilgus is advised to arrange publication through the Civil Information and Education Section in Tokyo and the War Department's Reorientation Branch. The State Department sees no objection on broader reorientation-policy grounds and has forwarded the letter and booklet to the War Department.

subfiles.title: Eleanor Roosevelt asks Acheson whether to acknowledge Nomura's book
subfiles.about: Roosevelt asks whether she should acknowledge the book that Compton Pakenham says he is sending on Admiral Nomura's behalf.
subfiles.summary: In a brief note, Eleanor Roosevelt forwards the matter to Dean Acheson for advice. She specifically asks whether she should acknowledge the book when it arrives.

subfiles.title: Compton Pakenham forwards Admiral Nomura's A Mission to America
subfiles.about: Pakenham reports that he is sending Roosevelt the Japanese edition of Admiral Nomura's book and conveys Nomura's condolences and regard.
subfiles.summary: Writing from Tokyo through occupation headquarters, Pakenham says that a copy of Nomura's Japanese edition, which he renders as A Mission to America, is being sent separately. He also conveys Nomura's belated condolences and highest regard. Pakenham explains that he is acting as intermediary because direct communication with the admiral is impossible and offers to pass any reply to him.

subfiles.title: Request to draft Acheson's reply to Eleanor Roosevelt
subfiles.from: Florence Kirlin, Office of the Under Secretary
subfiles.about: Kirlin asks Ringwalt to prepare a reply for Acheson's signature concerning A Mission to America.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum directs Mr. Ringwalt to draft an answer to Roosevelt's October 14 letter. It also requests a certified copy of the completed reply for the Office of the Under Secretary.

subfiles.title: Acting Secretary advises Roosevelt not to acknowledge Nomura's book
subfiles.from: Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Acheson recommends that Roosevelt take no further action because Pakenham's delivery of Nomura's book circumvents restrictions on mail to and from Japan.
subfiles.summary: The reply explains that existing mail restrictions prevent Admiral Nomura from sending the book directly from Japan. Although Pakenham apparently does not recognize the impropriety, the Department regards his intervention as a circumvention of those restrictions. Acheson shares Roosevelt's doubts and advises her not to acknowledge or otherwise pursue the matter; the copy bears a November 23 stamp and a November 21 drafting notation.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting SCAP regulations on foreign mass media
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Despatch No. 774 transmits copies of a SCAP circular regulating the admission and dissemination of foreign publications and mass media in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Political Adviser forwards five copies of a circular issued by General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, on December 5, 1946. The circular and its enclosures establish licensing procedures and rules for importing, distributing, and selling foreign books, magazines, films, news, and photographic services in Japan.

subfiles.title: SCAP Circular No. 12 on admission of foreign media
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Foreign missions and prospective foreign media licensees in Japan
subfiles.about: The circular announces the main occupation regulations for commercial and non-commercial foreign mass media entering Japan.
subfiles.summary: Foreign commercial media may enter Japan only under SCAP license and only when they are not detrimental to occupation purposes. The circular establishes separate rules for magazines, books, motion pictures, performance rights, and news and photograph services, including restrictions on foreign publishers operating directly in Japan. Non-commercial material may be imported only when useful to occupation information and education objectives and must be disseminated exclusively through headquarters. The circular is issued by command of General MacArthur and authenticated by Paul J. Mueller and John B. Cooley.

subfiles.title: License procedures for commercial foreign mass media
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Foreign media publishers, copyright owners, news services, and motion-picture industries
subfiles.about: Inclosure 1 prescribes the licensing procedure and financial conditions for foreign mass-media businesses operating in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Applicants must proceed through their national mission and the appropriate SCAP section, with American applicants using the Civil Information and Education Section. Contracts and payments must be in Japanese yen, which may be spent only on essential Japanese goods and services and cannot presently be converted into foreign exchange. Licensees may contract with Japanese nationals or conduct business through a Japanese agent once approval is granted.

subfiles.title: Regulations for translation, reproduction, and performance rights
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.to: Foreign copyright owners and Japanese publishers
subfiles.about: Inclosure 2 establishes the controlled channels for selling foreign translation, reproduction, and performance rights in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Licensed national publishing groups may sell rights but may not station representatives in Japan; a Japanese group and SCAP will handle business arrangements and correspondence. Books considered helpful to occupation objectives may be recommended and offered to Japanese publishers through competitive bidding, while SCAP may also solicit particular works. To conserve paper, harmless but non-contributory books must be matched by works that positively support occupation objectives. Proofs and copyright contracts must be submitted for Press Code censorship, and theatrical and musical performance rights follow the same system.

subfiles.title: Regulations for foreign commercial motion pictures
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Inclosure 3 regulates the importation, preparation, censorship, distribution, and exhibition of foreign commercial films in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Allied commercial films require licenses, and annual imports from each country are capped at that country's prewar maximum. Licensees must bring their own raw film and submit positive prints and English translations for evaluation by the Civil Information and Education Section. Completed Japanese-titled, subtitled, or dubbed versions are then subject to the Pictorial Censorship Code, while nonstandard uses such as charity performances require special approval.

subfiles.title: Regulations for non-commercial foreign mass media
subfiles.from: General Headquarters, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: Inclosure 4 places the importation and use of foreign non-commercial media under exclusive SCAP supervision.
subfiles.summary: Foreign non-commercial news, publications, photographs, films, and related materials may not be distributed to Japanese recipients outside SCAP channels. Allied missions may submit translated materials that support occupation objectives, but material advancing the separate interests of an individual government or nation will be rejected. Approved mass-distribution material remains subject to the occupation censorship codes.

subfiles.title: Department of State document charge-out record
subfiles.about: The sheet records the administrative charging and circulation of another numbered document among persons identified principally by surnames or initials.
subfiles.summary: Form DS-516 contains a file number, brief handwritten descriptions, and charge information involving L. Vann, L. Tang, and several unidentified initials. Its relationship to the substantive 1946 correspondence is not explained, but it documents later archival handling within the Department.

interest: The file is especially useful for showing how ordinary cultural transactions—translation of an American pamphlet, receipt of a Japanese admiral's memoir, or importation of a film—were entangled with occupation controls. The SCAP circular provides unusually detailed evidence of the administrative machinery behind cultural reorientation: licenses, blocked yen earnings, competitive bidding for copyrights, paper-allocation rules, and successive policy and censorship reviews. The Nomura–Roosevelt exchange adds a revealing personal dimension, demonstrating official sensitivity even to an apparently courteous private gift that bypassed restrictions on communication with Japan. The routing marks and final charge-out sheet also help reconstruct how such matters circulated through the State Department long after the original correspondence.
